issues.legal_issue: Commutation of hereditary service does not by itself change the tenure of land granted as watan property.
material_facts: The land had been granted as remuneration for hereditary village service, and the parties accepted that the grant was of the soil rather than merely a share of revenue.
Under a commutation settlement, the holder was relieved of the service obligation in return for paying a fixed sum.
No express agreement altering the tenure of the land was established.
issues.conclusion: The commutation relieved the holder and successors of the service obligation but did not, without an express agreement to that effect, change the land’s watan tenure; the watan and its restrictions continued subject to the settlement.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 4 and 15(1)–(3) of the Bombay Hereditary Offices Act, 1874, the watan comprises the watan property, hereditary office, and attached rights and privileges; an hereditary office retains its character even when its service is no longer demanded. Commutation relieves the service obligation but does not alter the tenure absent an express agreement. Section 22 permits the watan rights to be determined by resumption. The Court relied on Appaji Bapuji v. Keshav Shamrav, (1890) I.L.R. 15 Bom. 13, and Bachharam Datta Patil v. Viswanath Pundalik Patil, [1956] S.C.R. 675.

rule.if: watan_tenure_dispute and land_granted_for_hereditary_service and service_obligation_commuted and not express_tenure_change

predicates.watan_tenure_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether land granted for hereditary service retained its special tenure after the service obligation ended.
predicates.land_granted_for_hereditary_service: The land was granted as remuneration for duties attached to a hereditary office.
predicates.service_obligation_commuted: The holder agreed to a settlement under which the holder and successors were relieved of the service obligation.
predicates.express_tenure_change: The settlement expressly changed the tenure of the land.

issues.definition: When a dispute concerns land granted for hereditary service and a settlement ends the service obligation without expressly changing the tenure, the watan tenure continues.

issues.legal_issue: Legislative abolition of a hereditary watan extinguishes the office and alters the holder’s rights in the land as provided by the abolishing law.
material_facts: The abolishing legislation provided that the relevant watans were abolished, the rights to hold the hereditary office and the associated service liability were extinguished, and the watan land was resumed.
The rights were affected by legislative operation, rather than by an executive exercise of the power to confiscate or resume a watan.
issues.conclusion: The abolition, extinction, and modification of the holder’s rights followed from the statute that abolished the watan.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3 of the Bombay Pargana and Kulkarni Watans (Abolition) Act, 1950, abolished the specified watans, extinguished the rights to hold the office and the service liability, resumed the watan land subject to the Act, and extinguished the incidents of the watans. Where abolition occurs by legislative enactment rather than executive action, its consequences are determined by that enactment.

predicates.watan_abolition_effect_dispute: The proceeding concerns the effect of legislation abolishing a hereditary watan.
predicates.legislation_abolishes_the_watan_and_ends: The legislation abolishes the hereditary watan and provides for ending the associated office rights and altering the status of its land.

issues.definition: When a dispute concerns legislative abolition and the legislation abolishes the watan and ends its associated rights, those rights are extinguished or modified by law.

issues.legal_issue: A holder whose watan land is resumed and made available to the holder as occupancy land is not entitled to additional compensation under a residual compensation provision for loss of the watan rights in that land.
material_facts: The holder sought monetary compensation for the loss of rights in land granted as remuneration for hereditary service and also claimed a right to enjoy part of the land revenue.
The grant was accepted to be of the soil, not merely a cash allowance or a share of land revenue.
The abolition legislation provided for the resumed land to be regranted to the holder as occupancy land upon payment of the prescribed occupancy price.
The holder had not claimed the occupancy regrant; the Court expressly left open whether that omission affected entitlement to it.
issues.conclusion: The occupancy regrant provided compensation for the loss of the watan rights in the land, so the holder was not entitled to compensation under the residual provision for that loss. The Court did not decide whether the holder remained entitled to seek the regrant.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 3 and 4 of the Bombay Pargana and Kulkarni Watans (Abolition) Act, 1950, provide for resumption and regrant of watan land as occupancy land. Section 6 provides specified compensation for cash allowances and for land or a village whose watan property consists of all or part of its land revenue. Section 9(1) permits compensation for abolished, extinguished, or modified property rights only where the Act makes no other provision for compensation. The occupancy right under section 4, freed from the incidents of watan tenure, compensates for loss of the watan rights in the land; section 9 therefore does not provide additional monetary compensation for that loss.

predicates.compensation_claim_proceeding: A holder seeks compensation for rights or interests lost through abolition of a hereditary tenure.
predicates.land_granted_as_watan_remuneration: The land was granted as remuneration for hereditary service rather than solely as a cash allowance or share of land revenue.
predicates.occupancy_regrant_available_for_resumed_: After resumption, the law makes the land available to its former holder as occupancy land, subject to the required payment.

issues.definition: When a compensation claim concerns land granted as hereditary-service remuneration and the law makes an occupancy regrant available after resumption, no additional residual cash compensation is awarded for loss of the watan rights in that land.
